Christ teaches that one must deserve well of everyone, even loving enemies, giving loans freely, taking no vengeance on anyone, and giving to every petitioner. In contrast, the philosophers teach that one should give only to those who repay a benefit with a benefit; otherwise, it is permitted to be angry, to hate, to contend, to wage war, and to practice usury. Furthermore, they have handed down the Pelagian heretics <note>Followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human effort and free will over divine grace.</note> to us with their notions of free will, the dictates of right reason, and the light of nature. Indeed, all moral philosophy, as Lactantius <note>An early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> witnesses, is false and empty, neither instructing in the duties of justice, nor confirming the duty and reasons of man. Finally, it all contradicts the divine law and Christ himself, so that its glory is owed to none other than Satan.

## ON POLITICS
### Chapter 55

Politics also belongs to this branch of philosophy, which is the art of administering the <term>Republic</term> <gloss>the state or commonwealth</gloss>. Indeed, there are three types of it: namely, <term>Monarchy</term> <gloss>the rule of one</gloss>; <term>Aristocracy</term> <gloss>the rule of the few, but the noble,</gloss> <column-break/> the rich, or the wise; and <term>Democracy</term> <gloss>the rule of the people</gloss>. And related to all these are tyrannies, oligarchies, and anarchies. But all these things are to be referred to whatever happens to each person. For even if philosophers want to define which form is the best, they follow diverse opinions. Some, just as there is one God in heaven, one head among the limbs, and one leader among the bees, admit that monarchy is the preferable form of right government. Others contend that aristocracy, and others democracy, is the form of rule which is equal and by which liberty is preserved. This is argued especially by those such as Plato, Aristotle, Apuleius, and others, not only from among our own people, but even from the barbarians <note>Agrippa refers to non-Greek and non-Roman civilizations as barbarians, following classical custom.</note>. Those who have written about these things speak only of what pertains to external administration, peace, the tranquility of public affairs, and deliberation. They do not look to the soul, nor to salvation, nor to eternal aids, but look solely to those things that are performed in this world. <summary>Agrippa concludes his critique of moral philosophy by arguing it leads to heresy and serves Satan, then introduces politics by defining the three main types of government.</summary>
